metadata.title: ICT Engagement: a new construct and its assessment in PISA 2015

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses secondary public-use microdata from the OECD PISA 2015 main study for Switzerland and Germany, focusing on questionnaire-based ICT Engagement and ICT usage scales. The analyses are conducted in Mplus using the WLSMV estimator for categorical indicators and pairwise present data, which is a measurement-model approach rather than a PV-based achievement prediction pipeline. The manuscript does not report the application of PISA sampling weights (e.g., student design weights) or replicate-weight procedures, so population-representative inference for standard errors cannot be confirmed from the text. For replication, analysts should apply the official PISA 2015 complex survey design weights available in the OECD database when estimating uncertainty, and ensure the same questionnaire item inclusion rules for the ICT Engagement scale across countries.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 main study public-use data for Switzerland and Germany. The ICT Engagement and ICT usage constructs were derived from Likert questionnaire items (ICT Engagement: 4 subscales with 6/5/5/5 items; ICT usage: 4 motive aspects with 7 items for school use and 5/3/10 items for outside-of-school use). Missingness on ICT Engagement items differed by country (Swiss: 8.8–12.2% per item; German: 18.1–21.3% per item), and the authors report that 4593 German respondents (70.6%) had no missing value while 1105 (approx. 17%) provided no valid answer on ICT Engagement scales. For the correlations with PISA literacy performance, the authors conducted SEM analyses for five plausible values and averaged the results.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity (Switzerland) — ICT Engagement scale (4-factor measurement model)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Four-factor SEM fit: χ2=7650.9, df=179, CFI=0.929, RMSEA=0.087; latent correlations between factors ranged 0.44–0.79 (ICT competence–autonomy high, motivating a 4-factor model).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity data (Switzerland) the study leveraged ICT interest, perceived ICT competence, perceived autonomy in ICT use, and ICT as a topic in social interaction to model the ICT Engagement latent structure, finding that a four-dimensional measurement model fit the data acceptably (CFI=0.929; RMSEA=0.087) with distinct latent factors (correlations 0.44–0.79). This indicates that the ICT Engagement construct can be interpreted as four separable subscales for subsequent validity and policy-relevant monitoring of students’ ICT-related motivation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity (Switzerland) — ICT usage motives (latent regression)
main_findings.target_variable: ICT usage motives (variance explained by ICT Engagement)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Latent regression SEM fit: χ2=18257.7, df=904, CFI=0.905, RMSEA=0.058. Explained variance in ICT usage outside school: Use for Entertainment 74.1% (SE=2.8%), Practical usage 21.8% (SE=1.3%), Learning-related use at home 10.8% (SE=1%). Explained variance in ICT usage at school: 8.7% (SE=0.9%). Predictive pattern: ICT as social interaction had highest predictive values for almost all motives except Practical usage; perceived ICT competence did not significantly contribute when controlling for other ICT Engagement aspects.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity data (Switzerland) the study leveraged the four ICT Engagement subscales to predict latent ICT usage motives, finding that ICT Engagement explained substantially more variance in self-chosen outside-of-school entertainment use (74.1%) than in learning-related home use (10.8%) and only modest variance in ICT use at school (8.7%). This indicates that interventions aiming to increase students’ ICT engagement may be more effective for boosting voluntary, entertainment- and practical-oriented ICT use than for changing school-driven ICT use.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity (Switzerland) — Gender differences in ICT Engagement
main_findings.target_variable: ICT Engagement latent means by gender
main_findings.performance_metrics: Measurement invariance: scalar invariance rejected (ΔCFI=0.016; DIFFTEST p<0.001). Female vs male latent mean differences (male reference=0): perceived ICT competence M=-0.47 (p<0.001), perceived ICT autonomy M=-0.58 (p<0.001), ICT social interaction topic M=-0.80 (p<0.001); ICT interest M=-0.05 (p=0.07, not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity data (Switzerland) the study leveraged gender-group comparisons of the ICT Engagement latent means, finding that girls scored significantly lower than boys on perceived ICT competence, perceived autonomy in ICT use, and ICT as a topic in social interaction, while ICT interest showed no significant gender difference (p=0.07). This indicates that gender-responsive support should prioritize competence and autonomy-related ICT engagement components, while recognizing that interest may be less gender-differentiated.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 literacy (Switzerland) — Correlations with ICT Engagement and ICT usage
main_findings.performance_metrics: Averaged across five plausible values: ICT as social interaction topic vs reading r=-0.20 (Switzerland); ICT autonomy vs mathematics r=0.17 (Switzerland). ICT usage vs performance: practical usage vs mathematics r=0.14 and vs science r=0.13; ICT use at school vs reading r=-0.20; school/learning-related use at home vs reading r=-0.21.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 literacy data (Switzerland) the study leveraged ICT Engagement and ICT usage constructs to estimate SEM-based correlations with reading performance (averaged across five plausible values), finding a small but statistically negative association between ICT as a topic in social interaction and reading performance (r=-0.20). This indicates that students with lower reading performance may rely more on social ICT exchange for help or problem-solving, suggesting that digital learning supports should be designed to complement reading skill development rather than substituting for it.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity (Germany) — ICT Engagement scale (replication of 4-factor structure)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Switzerland–Germany measurement invariance for ICT Engagement: scalar invariance established using ΔCFI criterion (ΔCFI=0.002 ≤ 0.01) with configural CFI=0.935 and scalar CFI=0.933; model fit for scalar structure: χ2=14925, df=413, CFI=0.933, RMSEA=0.080.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity data (Germany) the study leveraged the same four ICT Engagement subscales to test cross-country measurement equivalence with Switzerland, finding that scalar invariance could be established (ΔCFI=0.002) and that the four-factor structure remained comparable across countries. This indicates that ICT Engagement subscales can support cross-country comparisons of students’ ICT-related motivation components, enabling more consistent monitoring of digital engagement gaps.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 literacy (Germany) — Correlations with ICT Engagement and ICT usage
main_findings.performance_metrics: Averaged across five plausible values: ICT as social interaction topic vs reading r=-0.12 (Germany); ICT use at school vs mathematics r=-0.23; ICT use at school vs reading r=-0.27; school/learning-related use at home vs reading r=-0.15.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 literacy data (Germany) the study leveraged ICT Engagement and ICT usage constructs to estimate SEM-based correlations with reading performance (averaged across five plausible values), finding a small negative association between ICT as a topic in social interaction and reading performance (r=-0.12). This indicates that the relationship between socially oriented ICT engagement and reading achievement is not limited to one country, supporting the need for education practices that integrate social ICT use with literacy scaffolding.

data.outcome_summary: This study provides construct validity evidence for the newly introduced PISA 2015 ICT Engagement scale, using PISA 2015 main-study questionnaire data from Switzerland (n=5860) and Germany (n=6504). The authors estimated SEM measurement models in Mplus (WLSMV for ordinal indicators) and confirmed a four-dimensional ICT Engagement structure (ICT interest, perceived ICT competence, perceived autonomy in ICT use, and ICT as a topic in social interaction) with acceptable fit in Switzerland (CFI=0.929; RMSEA=0.087). In a latent regression model, ICT Engagement explained substantially more variance in outside-of-school entertainment use (74.1%) than in learning-related home use (10.8%) and only modest variance in ICT use at school (8.7%). Gender comparisons showed lower latent means for girls on competence, autonomy, and social-interaction engagement (with scalar invariance not fully supported). Correlations with PISA literacy performance were small; notably, ICT social interaction topic correlated negatively with reading (r=-0.20 in Switzerland; r=-0.12 in Germany). Limitations include the absence of documented survey-weight application and the cross-sectional design, so results support validity and associations rather than causal effects.
